items.stem: A team is investigating newly arrived migrant families in the town struggling to access services. Explain why each member should research a different perspective on the problem.
items.answer: It ensures a range of perspectives (e.g. students, local officials, organisations working on international migration, including migration linked to conflict and climate change) is covered without duplication, and each member then brings distinct evidence to the team’s discussion of solutions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark coverage of perspectives; 1 mark avoids duplication/efficiency; 1 mark improves the solution [3]

items.stem: A team is investigating young people having no say in decisions made by the town council. Explain why each member should research a different perspective on the problem.

items.stem: A team planning a project on low turnout in student council elections at a school lists these tasks: A agree the problem and roles (4 days); B individual research on perspectives (6 days, after A); C survey of students (3 days, after A, can run at the same time as B); D agree the solution (3 days, after both B and C). What is the shortest time in which all tasks can be completed?
items.answer: 13 days

items.stem: A team planning a project on lack of trust in the honesty of local officials lists these tasks: A agree the problem and roles (3 days); B individual research on perspectives (5 days, after A); C survey of students (3 days, after A, can run at the same time as B); D agree the solution (3 days, after both B and C). Calculate the shortest completion time and identify the sequence of tasks that determines it.
items.answer: 3 + max(5, 3) + 3 = 11 days; critical sequence A → B → D.
items.markingKey: 1 mark recognises B and C run in parallel; 1 mark total; 1 mark critical sequence [3]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the success of a team project depends more on good planning than on the abilities of individual members? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: A clear plan with roles and deadlines prevents duplication and missed tasks. Planning lets the team combine research on different perspectives. Against: Skilled, motivated members can overcome a weak plan. Communication and trust matter as much as planning. Judgement: Planning provides the framework, but success also needs commitment and communication; e.g. a team addressing newly arrived migrant families in the town struggling to access services needs both.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: A team compares three solutions to low turnout in student council elections at a school. Solution | Cost ($) | People reached. introduce online voting for student elections | 600 | 60. hold candidate debates during lessons | 150 | 400. run a peer campaign explaining how the council has changed school life | 600 | 300. Calculate the cost per person reached for each solution and identify the most cost-effective.
items.answer: introduce online voting for student elections: $10; hold candidate debates during lessons: $0.38; run a peer campaign explaining how the council has changed school life: $2. Most cost-effective: hold candidate debates during lessons.

Calculate the cost per person reached for each solution and identify the most cost-effective.
items.answer: replace single-use packaging with reusable containers: $0.75; set up a recycling scheme with a local firm: $2.67; run a student awareness campaign: $3.75. Most cost-effective: replace single-use packaging with reusable containers.

items.stem: A team compares three solutions to newly arrived migrant families in the town struggling to access services. Solution | Cost ($) | People reached. create a multilingual guide to local services | 150 | 80. organise a student buddy scheme for new families | 200 | 300. ask the council to provide interpreters at its offices | 300 | 120. Calculate the cost per person reached for each solution and identify the most cost-effective. Explain why the most cost-effective solution may not be the best one to recommend.
items.answer: create a multilingual guide to local services: $1.88; organise a student buddy scheme for new families: $0.67; ask the council to provide interpreters at its offices: $2.5. Most cost-effective: organise a student buddy scheme for new families. Cost per person ignores how much each person is helped and how lasting the effect is; e.g. its weakness: it depends on volunteers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method (cost ÷ people); 1 mark all values; 1 mark identification; 1 mark effectiveness/depth of impact; 1 mark applies a weakness of the solution [5]

items.stem: A team proposes to share a simple checklist for verifying posts to address misleading health and election rumours shared in a neighbourhood messaging group. Explain one strength and one weakness of this solution.
items.answer: Strength: it is cheap and easy to spread. Weakness: people may ignore it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength, 1 mark developed; 1 mark weakness, 1 mark developed [4]

items.stem: A team proposes to set up a youth advisory council to address young people having no say in decisions made by the town council. Explain one strength and one weakness of this solution.
items.answer: Strength: young people are consulted regularly. Weakness: the council may ignore its advice.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strength, 1 mark developed; 1 mark weakness, 1 mark developed [4]

items.stem: A team compares three solutions to misleading health and election rumours shared in a neighbourhood messaging group. Solution | Cost ($) | People reached. run media literacy workshops at the community centre | 150 | 300. appoint volunteer “fact-check champions” in the group | 800 | 300. share a simple checklist for verifying posts | 150 | 80. Calculate the cost per person reached for each solution and identify the most cost-effective.
items.answer: run media literacy workshops at the community centre: $0.5; appoint volunteer “fact-check champions” in the group: $2.67; share a simple checklist for verifying posts: $1.88. Most cost-effective: run media literacy workshops at the community centre.
items.markingKey: 1 mark method (cost ÷ people); 1 mark all values; 1 mark identification [3]

items.stem: A team in Dhaka has researched young people having no say in decisions made by the town council, which links to under-representation of young people in governance worldwide. They are choosing between two solutions: to reserve a seat for a youth representative at council meetings, or to set up a youth advisory council. Explain one advantage of the first solution.
items.answer: Young people are present when decisions are made.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Assess the claim that the best way to address newly arrived migrant families in the town struggling to access services is to ask the council to provide interpreters at its offices.
items.answer: For: It helps with complex official matters. It responds to a local example of international migration, including migration linked to conflict and climate change. Against: It is costly for the council. Other solutions may reach more people or last longer. Judgement: A justified recommendation compares solutions on effectiveness, cost, feasibility and acceptability, using research evidence.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the best way to address young people having no say in decisions made by the town council is to hold a youth consultation online before major decisions? Consider different perspectives in your answer.
items.answer: For: Many people can take part. It responds to a local example of under-representation of young people in governance worldwide. Against: Responses may not be representative. Other solutions may reach more people or last longer. Judgement: A justified recommendation compares solutions on effectiveness, cost, feasibility and acceptability, using research evidence.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–3 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (4–6 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (7–9 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [9]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which term matches this definition: “a small card with key points used as a prompt while speaking”? (b) What is meant by “presentation” in Global Perspectives?
items.answer: (a) Cue card (b) A spoken explanation of research and a proposed solution, supported by visual aids.
items.markingKey: (a) Cue card: a small card with key points used as a prompt while speaking. [1] (b) Presentation: a spoken explanation of research and a proposed solution, supported by visual aids. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a student presenting a solution to misleading health and election rumours shared in a neighbourhood messaging group should cite sources on the slides.
items.answer: It shows the evidence is credible and avoids plagiarism.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reason; 1 mark developed [2]

items.stem: Mei is preparing an individual presentation on the team’s proposal to introduce online voting for student elections to address low turnout in student council elections at a school. The first draft has twelve slides full of text and no sources. Outline a suitable structure for the presentation.
items.answer: Problem and its global dimension → research findings and perspectives → solution and justification → conclusion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark logical order; 1 mark includes justification [2]

items.stem: Yusuf speaks at about 150 words per minute and has a script of 1,400 words for a presentation that must last no more than 8 minutes. Calculate how long the script would take and how many words must be cut, if any.
items.answer: 1,400 ÷ 150 = 9.3 minutes; maximum = 1,200 words, so cut 200 words.
items.markingKey: 1 mark time; 1 mark maximum words; 1 mark words to cut [3]

items.stem: “A presentation is a better way than a written report to communicate a proposed solution to plastic waste from the school canteen.” Discuss this claim, considering arguments for and against before reaching a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: It can engage an audience directly, using visuals and voice. The speaker can adapt to the audience. Against: A written report can include more evidence and detailed referencing. Readers can return to it and check sources. Judgement: Each suits different purposes; the presentation must still show credible evidence and justification.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–5 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (6–8 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [8]

items.stem: A student’s reflective paper on a project about misleading health and election rumours shared in a neighbourhood messaging group says: “We met, did our research, made a presentation and finished on time.” Explain why this is description rather than reflection, and how it could be improved.
items.answer: It only reports what happened; reflection evaluates what went well or badly, analyses why, and states what the writer learned and will do differently (e.g. how roles were shared and what that taught them).
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies description only; 1 mark what reflection adds (evaluation/analysis); 1 mark suggests improvement [3]

items.stem: A student’s reflective paper on a project about lack of trust in the honesty of local officials says: “We met, did our research, made a presentation and finished on time.” Explain why this is description rather than reflection, and how it could be improved.
items.answer: It only reports what happened; reflection evaluates what went well or badly, analyses why, and states what the writer learned and will do differently (e.g. how roles were shared and what that taught them).
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies description only; 1 mark what reflection adds (evaluation/analysis); 1 mark suggests improvement [3]

items.stem: A student is writing a reflective paper after a team project on newly arrived migrant families in the town struggling to access services. The team’s solution was well received, but there was conflict over roles in the first two weeks. Write one sentence of analysis about the conflict.
items.answer: e.g. “The conflict arose because we had not agreed roles, so two of us researched the same perspective.”
items.markingKey: 1 mark cause identified; 1 mark explained [2]
